title: Cheesecake, peptides and a defection: the last week before the vote, unwrapped
dek: A Michigan Democrat endorses the Republican, the White House goes to war with a restaurant, HHS overrules its own scientists, and Iran talks get measured in minutes.
body:
## Michigan: the call is coming from inside the party

Tomorrow is Election Day, which means it is the traditional moment for a party to come together, set aside its differences and absolutely not endorse the other guy. Michigan Democrats went a different way.

On Sunday, Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in August, endorsed the Republican, Mike Rogers [1]. Her explanation, in a video on X: "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right" [1]. Then she appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church [2]. The fight began over an ad by an outside group linking U.S. military aid to Israel to grocery prices; Stevens called it antisemitic, and El-Sayed said the ad "was not made by me" and that he disagreed with it, while accusing her of "relitigating a primary that ended three months ago" [2].

Rogers called her "a courageous leader" [2]. Her chief of staff of eight years and several other aides quit, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a "despicable betrayal," adding, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens" [1]. Which is a funny thing to say about a candidate the Senate Democrats' campaign arm had heavily backed in the primary [2]. Nothing says "I don't think about you" like a press availability about how much you don't think about someone. The Washington Examiner reported she had been kicked out of her state party [3]. Michigan Democrats: proving every cycle that the circular firing squad is a renewable resource.

## The Cheesecake Factory: the only winner of the midterms so far

Elsewhere, the closing argument of the 2026 campaign turned out to be a restaurant. Barack Obama, campaigning in Ohio, compared the gilded White House to Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory [4]. A normal administration lets that go. This one mobilized. Trump said Obama "wouldn't understand" the renovations, called the chain "a very successful company" and said the cost was "peanuts" [5]. The White House's own accounts posted AI-generated images of Trump outside a Cheesecake Factory, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent staged a photo op eating there [6]. The Treasury secretary. During a war. With prices up. Eating there. For content.

Obama, to his credit as a comedian and debit as a man who ever has to stop talking, came back to the bit days later in Georgia, saying he had been a Cheesecake Factory regular for about a decade [11]. The company itself said nothing, ignored the whole thing on its earnings call and went quiet on Instagram [6]. It then reported a record quarter, with $1.03 billion in revenue [7]. A president and a former president fought, and the only entity that came out ahead was the one that didn't post.

## HHS: freedom, now with a comment period

On Wednesday, the Department of Health and Human Services told compounding pharmacies they could make six unapproved injectable "wellness" peptides, including BPC-157, without facing enforcement, while the FDA writes rules [8][9]. An HHS spokesperson was careful to say the policy "does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness" [9]. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said it "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety" [9].

The Associated Press reported that HHS first wanted the FDA to write a formal rule, but FDA officials warned that the agency's scientists had major safety concerns and wouldn't support one, so HHS switched to a route that sidesteps them [8]. Kennedy has said he used BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury [8]. So, to recap: the experts said no, the boss said he tried it and felt great, and the policy went ahead anyway. That's not drug regulation. That's a group chat. Public comment runs through November 13 [9], so if you have feelings, there's a form.

## Iran: ten minutes, one or two sites, zero hurry

And over the weekend, the war that was supposed to be wrapping up announced it might not be. At Mar-a-Lago, Trump said the U.S. had "knocked out" Iran's nuclear program but still had to take care of "one or two sites," adding, "we can do that in 10 minutes" [10]. He said talks were "going fine but you know they're not very reliable" [10]. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision on new strikes had been made [10].

Iran's side was not exactly cooling things down. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told commanders any threat "must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," and a top security official said the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz would continue until Iran's conditions are met [10]. So both governments are publicly describing a war in terms of how fast they could make it worse. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating; no lasting deal has been reached [10]. The two most reassuring words in the region right now are "Qatari mediators," which is not a sentence anyone expected to write.

## Tomorrow

Polls open in the morning. If you're voting, the stakes are high: Congress, governors and, since Trump had warned an attack on Iran could come after the midterms, possibly the war itself [10]. Also whatever the White House decides to start a fight with next. The Cheesecake Factory has already won. Everyone else has to wait for the count.
targets: President Trump and the White House
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
